item.title: Conditional Mean Flows for Frequency-Domain Scattered Wavefield Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.31071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frequency-domain wavefield modeling underpins seismic imaging and inversion, where repeated Helmholtz solutions become costly as velocity models, source locations, and frequencies vary. Neural operators learn mappings between physical fields, and their accuracy can decline outside the training distribution. Diffusion models learn wavefield distributions and generally require repeated sampling evaluations to produce accurate fields. A conditional mean flows model is introduced for complex scattered-wavefield generation. The analytical background wavefield serves as a condition alongside the velocity model, supplying spatially organized information about the source location and frequency. Learning the scattered wavefield avoids the point-source singularity in the target and supports generalization across these physical conditions. The model estimates the average transport velocity over a finite interval connecting Gaussian noise to the scattered field. This representation captures the accumulated displacement and permits both full-interval one-step generation and interval-partitioned sampling. Trained on OpenFWI, the model is evaluated on in-distribution and out-of-distribution velocity structures, frequency generalization, and inference efficiency. In most evaluated settings, one-step mean flows sampling achieves lower wavefield error than multi-step diffusion. Because each sampling step requires another network evaluation, accurate one-step generation also reduces inference time. These results indicate that mean flows can provide accurate and efficient frequency-domain scattered-wavefield generation.
item.dc:creator: Lipeng Lai, Shaohuan Zu

item.title: GeoAgent: Contract-Constrained LLM Agents for Seismic Data Processing
item.description: arXiv:2610.31096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can drive scientific software through function calling, but free-form tool use is fragile on long, data-dependent processing chains. Models omit arguments, invent units, feed the previous artifact into the wrong input, and report completion without a verifiable product. We present GeoAgent, an agent system for seismic data processing built on Madagascar's roughly 1{,}965 command-line programs. GeoAgent exposes 54 operator agents (51 generated from a declarative specification), retrieves from an index of 1{,}937 operators, and encodes the processing flow as a nine-stage state graph. Four explicit contracts---named artifacts, input resolution, parameter takeover, and artifact validation---move everything the graph can determine out of the model's discretion. A deterministic geometry tool parses the self-describing SPS/RPS/XPS and SEG-Y headers, cross-checks eight consistency conditions, and reproduces the reference shell recipe exactly. The system runs in containers with session- and task-level isolation, bounded execution, and defenses against silent failures. On a 2-D land dataset, the nine-stage pipeline completes in about six to eleven minutes and yields a verified artifact at every stage, while retrieval reduces per-turn tool context from about 12k to 2k tokens. We report the design, deployment experience, and motivating failure modes.
item.dc:creator: Zhilong Fang, Qi Zhang, Jujie Yan, Zhong Wang, Xinbin Gu, Ziyang Zhang, Hua Wang

item.title: Modelling wide-swath altimeter observation-error correlations with a regularised diffusion operator
item.description: arXiv:2610.31409v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unaccounted-for observation-error correlations have long been known to be detrimental to the quality of atmospheric and ocean analyses produced by data assimilation (DA) systems. While progress has been made over the past decade on modelling inter-channel error correlations, modelling spatial error correlations remains a challenge for large datasets. Common strategies for mitigating the harmful effects of spatial error correlations, such as variance inflation or data thinning, prevent the extraction of valuable small-scale information from the observations. With the emergence of new sources of high-resolution observations, such as those from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) wide-swath altimeter, the need to address this limitation of DA systems has become increasingly pressing. To do so, we consider a diffusion-based observation-error correlation operator, extending previous work on modelling correlated errors in conventional nadir altimeter data. When observation-error correlation length scales are large, the original method can suffer from an excessive sensitivity of the inverse correlation operator to small-scale perturbations. Since actual estimates of observation-error correlations from SWOT suggest the presence of large length scales, a more robust formulation of the method is required. We present a regularised formulation of the diffusion-based correlation operator that eliminates this excessive sensitivity while preserving computational efficiency. We describe the implementation of the operator for a mesh constructed from SWOT observation locations and demonstrate its application in a global ocean DA system. To validate the new formulation, we perform DA experiments with simulated SWOT observations. These experiments confirm that the regularised correlation operator provides an effective, robust and practical approach for representing wide-swath altimeter observation-error correlations in operational ocean DA systems.
item.dc:creator: Olivier Goux (CERFACS), Anthony Weaver (CERFACS, CECI), Andrea Piacentini (CERFACS)

item.title: First Results of Calculation of the Dayside Magnetopause Reconnection Rate with TRACERS
item.description: arXiv:2610.30517v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantifying the rate of reconnection remains a key challenge in the study of geomagnetic storms. In this study, we present the first results from the new Tandem Reconnection and Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites (TRACERS) mission to calculate the reconnection rate from dispersed ion populations measured in the cusp, using previously developed methodology. We study ion dispersion events in two storms. During the first storm, which occurred on September 30, 2025, 21 dispersion events were identified in TRACERS 2 ion data as a combined result of geospace dynamics and the spacecraft cusp encounters. Throughout this time when ion dispersion was detected by TRACERS , the reconnection rate is calculated and is shown to track reasonably well with another measure of geomagnetic activity, the Cross Polar Cap Potential (CPCP) as obtained by the Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARN). The dispersions are correlated with the smoothed CPCP, and a correlation of $r^2=0.62$ was found using the dispersions from the onset and main phase of the storm. The correlation disappears when including dispersions from the recovery period. The distribution of reconnection rates throughout this storm lies generally between 0.1 - 1.5 mV/m, slightly lower than previous reconnection rates calculated with DMSP, but consistent with in-situ observations made with Polar. In this work, we also apply a previously developed automatic identification algorithm for ion-energy cusp dispersion to TRACERS, with the intent that it may serve as a tool for future statistical analysis as the data volume becomes too large to manually review.

item.title: Linear and nonlinear stability of rate-and-state faults
item.description: arXiv:2512.18729v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Models of faults incorporating slip rate- and state-dependent friction have reproduced phenomena from spontaneous slow, aseismic slip to earthquake-generating dynamic rupture. Numerical explorations of model parameter space show sudden transitions in behavior. However these boundaries are poorly constrained analytically, with commonly used scalings derived assuming unrepresentative conditions of uniform sliding on an infinite, homogeneous fault. In this work, we demonstrate that an analysis of linear stability can reflect model conditions. We examine two scenarios that move beyond the classical case: an asperity driven by the steady creep of its surroundings, and a finite fault experiencing a constant rate of shear loading. We identify the critical fault dimension $L_c$ at which point linear stability is lost. Beyond this linear regime, the non-linear nature of the friction law implies the loss of memory of loading conditions as instability progresses and the existence of universal solutions describing this process. We refine prior analyses of this non-linear instability and find the minimum fault size that can support self-sustaining, unstable acceleration towards dynamic rupture. We examine the role of the state evolution law and delineate conditions under which faults may be linearly stable but non-linearly unstable, requiring finitely large perturbations to trigger instability. For both the linear and non-linear analysis, we consider scenarios of two- and three-dimensional deformation. On the basis of numerical solutions, approximate but accurate algebraic expressions for the transition boundaries are presented. These results provide means for careful model design and to delimit plausible regions of parameter space when considering physical observations of stable creep, aseismic (slow slip) or seismic transients.
item.dc:creator: Robert C. Viesca, Dmitry I. Garagash

item.title: Evaluating Neural Probabilistic Forecasts of Sparse Earthquake Counts: What Survives a Careful Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2605.21437v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We revisit a neural negative binomial model for weekly earthquake counts on a 3 x 3 degree grid over the Tian Shan and Pamir, and ask which of its conclusions survive a careful evaluation. At the completeness magnitude of 4.5, the 144-week test period holds 2448 cell-weeks; six cell-weeks, in five distinct weeks, have three or more events. Two conclusions survive. First, Poisson forecasts, temporal ETAS included, understate the probability of such a busy week: ETAS expects 0.72 where six occurred, a shortfall by a factor of 8.3 (p = 0.00009, exact test). One dispersion parameter removes it (ETAS with dispersion expects 4.45, p = 0.58); simulating aftershock chains within the week also reproduces the tail but overshoots the total count by about a quarter. Second, the network's advantage over a linear model disappears once that model has an intercept per cell: the remaining gain is 3.4% of deviance, not significant (p = 0.57 over five test years), and it comes from one cell-week out of the 4420 scored; without it the network is 0.7% worse. A blind test on 2024 to September 2026, with every model fitted on data through 2023, confirms the tail result: Poisson forecasts are rejected (p from 3 x 10^-8 to 0.001), dispersion models are not (p between 0.25 and 0.84), except the NB GLM, whose level blew up out of sample and which is rejected at p = 0.003. Out of sample, model families differ in how they extrapolate beyond the training range, not in the per-cell term. We also measure the evaluation traps met on the way: a biased reference level, a single seed (five of six effects in v1's results table change sign), too few bootstrap resamples, and a threshold below completeness, which shrinks the ETAS shortfall from 8.3 to 2.8 times. This version replaces preprint v1; Section 7 lists the corrections.
item.dc:creator: Alim Igilik

item.title: Order-Disorder in Fe-Si Alloys: Implications for Seismic and Transport Properties of Earth's Inner Core
item.description: arXiv:2511.22899v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding the structure and dynamics of Earth's inner core is essential for constraining its composition, thermal evolution, and seismic behavior. Silicon is widely considered a major light element in the core. Here, we use first-principles molecular dynamics and thermodynamic modeling to investigate the structural, elastic, and transport properties of iron-silicon (Fe-Si) alloys under inner-core conditions. By computing the Gibbs free energies of multiple solid phases, including ordered B2, hexagonal close-packed (hcp), face-centered cubic (fcc), and body-centered cubic (bcc) Fe-Si, we construct a phase diagram relevant to inner-core pressures and temperatures. We identify a pronounced miscibility gap between hcp and cubic Fe--Si phases, with phase coexistence over approximately 6--11 wt\% Si at 6000 K. The cubic phase exhibits a strong order-dependent elastic response, with disordered bcc showing a large intrinsic shear anisotropy (22.9\% at 6000 K), in contrast to the nearly isotropic hcp phase (0.6\%). Meanwhile, disordered bcc Fe--Si produces shear wave velocities ($V_S=3.73$ km$\cdot$s$^{-1}$) and Poisson's ratios comparable with seismological constraints. In addition, disordered bcc Fe--Si exhibits a lower thermal conductivity than hcp Fe--Si, providing a quantitative constraint on phase-dependent electronic heat transport. These results demonstrate that chemical ordering strongly controls the stability and physical properties of cubic Fe--Si alloys, and suggest that metastable or localized cubic Fe--Si phases may contribute to the structural and transport complexity of Earth's inner core.
item.dc:creator: Cong Liu, Xin Deng, R. E. Cohen
